reference.source: OMIM / GeneReviews Primary Pyruvate Dehydrogenase Complex Deficiency
clinicalPearls: Pyruvate dehydrogenase phosphatase deficiency is a rare autosomal recessive cause of pyruvate dehydrogenase complex dysfunction, usually from PDP1 mutations
The phosphatase normally dephosphorylates and thereby activates the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, so its loss leaves the complex locked in an inactive, phosphorylated state
The result is impaired conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, with accumulation of pyruvate and lactate and a characteristically normal or low lactate-to-pyruvate ratio
Presentation is with neonatal or infantile lactic acidosis, hypotonia, feeding difficulty, developmental delay and, in some, features overlapping Leigh syndrome
Because the block is at the entry to the citric acid cycle, glucose loading tends to worsen lactic acidosis, whereas fat is a useful alternative fuel

Thiamine is a cofactor of the complex and a trial of generic thiamine supplementation is standard, and a high-fat, low-carbohydrate ketogenic dietary approach is used under specialist supervision to bypass the block
Diagnosis rests on demonstrating reduced pyruvate dehydrogenase complex activity that is restorable, with confirmation by PDP1 genetics
reference.pathophysiology: The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex links glycolysis to the citric acid cycle by converting pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, and its activity is regulated by reversible phosphorylation: pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase inactivates it and pyruvate dehydrogenase phosphatase reactivates it. In this disorder, recessive mutations (typically in PDP1) render the phosphatase deficient, so the complex remains phosphorylated and inactive. Pyruvate cannot be efficiently oxidised, so it and lactate accumulate while acetyl-CoA supply to the citric acid cycle falls, starving the brain of energy. Because pyruvate is diverted to lactate at the level of pyruvate rather than through a redox imbalance, the lactate-to-pyruvate ratio is usually normal or low, helping to distinguish it from respiratory-chain defects.
additionalDifferentials: Pyruvate dehydrogenase complex E1 (PDHA1) and other component deficiencies
Respiratory-chain (oxidative phosphorylation) disorders and Leigh syndrome
Organic acidaemias and fatty acid oxidation defects causing lactic acidosis
Secondary lactic acidosis from hypoxia or sepsis
additionalInvestigations: Blood and cerebrospinal fluid lactate and pyruvate with calculation of the lactate-to-pyruvate ratio
Pyruvate dehydrogenase complex enzyme activity assay in cultured fibroblasts, with and without conditions favouring dephosphorylation
Molecular genetic testing of PDP1 and other pyruvate dehydrogenase complex genes
Brain MRI, which may show basal ganglia or Leigh-type changes and structural anomalies
Plasma amino acids and urine organic acids to exclude other causes of lactic acidosis
Assessment of response to a supervised ketogenic dietary trial and thiamine
redFlags: Severe neonatal lactic acidosis with metabolic decompensation
Rapid neurological deterioration during intercurrent illness
reference.prognosis: Prognosis varies with residual enzyme activity: severe neonatal presentations carry high mortality and significant neurodisability, whereas milder cases may stabilise with dietary and cofactor management, though neurological impairment often persists.
pitfalls: Treating lactic acidosis with glucose-rich fluids, which can worsen it when the block is at pyruvate oxidation
Not distinguishing this from respiratory-chain disorders, which typically raise the lactate-to-pyruvate ratio
Failing to trial thiamine and a supervised ketogenic dietary approach that can bypass the metabolic block
Overlooking the enzyme assay conditions needed to reveal a phosphatase (activation) defect rather than a primary complex defect
